description:
We’re Team Green Line, and we built Greenline for the Field Shift challenge. Most farming advice fits an average farm, not the farmer's own. We combine NASA satellite and climate data with machine learning and a crop simulator to show how rotations hold up on their own field, through drought years and out to 2040.

Our team brings:

ML & Modeling (crop, weather and risk models)

Data Engineering (NASA and USDA data)

Simulation & Design (a playable farm simulator)

We show our work, failures included.
summary: Greenline is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) web app for phones, tablets and computers that helps North Texas farmers compare crop rotations for their own field using NASA Earth observation data. A farmer taps a field on a satellite map of six counties (1,711 sampled fields), searches an address or uses GPS (never stored), ranks their priorities, and gets up to 30 rotation options and three best plans outputted by our 5 custom trained models, each with evidence and uncertainty. NASA Satellite datasets such as but not limited to Landsat, HLS, SMAP, GPM IMERG, MODIS and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections are combined with USDA soil, crop and yield records. Five machine-learning models (crop history, drought and heat response, season types and 2040 climate, soil moisture, yield calibration) feed a transparent daily engine for water, growth, erosion, soil carbon, nitrogen and pests, tested against 1,000 what-if weather and price scenarios. We also provide a 2D Farm Simulator game on four plots with real past weather to allow farmers to better understand how their crops fare under various stressors.  It answers Field Shift by turning NASA data into local adaptation choices as drought and heat increase (8 of 8 climate models agree). It supports farmers and local experts instead of replacing them.
details:
What exactly does it do?
Greenline is an end-to-end tool that advises and helps aid decision making on selecting crop rotations by demonstrating how a specific crop rotation performs on a farmers specific field. The farmer first selects their field, chooses priorities, goals, restrictions and current crop rotation, then receives the 3 best crop rotation plans generated by our trained models that satisfy their specifications. They can then test rotations in our simulator powered by models to understand how they perform in future years and in specific conditions such as droughts.

How does it work?
Greenline covers 1,711 real farm fields in six North Texas counties. Five trained models: a boosted-tree and neural-network crop classifier names the crop on each field every year since 1985 (83% on unseen years against a 43% baseline), a sensitivity model measures how each field’s crops respond to drought and heat, a climate model labels each year drought, hot, wet or normal and projects how often each will occur around 2040, a soil-moisture model sets the starting soil water, and a yield model calibrates harvests to county records. These feed a daily crop water-balance engine that grows each crop through the season and tracks rain, soil water, stress, yield, bare soil, erosion and nitrogen. For every field, an optimizer builds up to 30 rotations and tests each one against 41 real seasons, 1,000 what-if seasons weighted toward 2040, and four fit checks for water, disease, markets and timing. The results become six scores (profit, risk, soil, water, nutrients and pests), weighted by the farmer’s priorities, with three best plans suggested.

What benefits does it have?
Our unique and custom trained models can predict per farm yield expectations based on plant structure, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, surface temperature, water stress, rainfall, underground water, elevation and many other factors derived from the data sets. Each prediction is unique to the specific farm region and provides the farmers with potential plans of action while still letting them make the final decisions. Additionally, they have the capability to tune for their specific needs, whether it be maximizing profit or saving as much water as possible. Farmers can also test potential rotations in our simulator game, where they can get a feel for growing the crops through seasons without being forced to commit. Every number shows its data source, and a one-page summary goes to the county extension agent.

What do you hope to achieve?
We want to be able to mitigate some of the risks that farmers have when getting started for a harvest season. It can be very difficult to predict some of the long term effects of your crop rotations on yields without having an extensive knowledge of agriculture, and even then it can be completely different based on where your field is located. Our goal is to remove this uncertainty from farmers through unique but applicable calculations and a custom simulation. With widespread use, this can lead to greater income and yield stability for independent farmers, a group that makes up 96% of US Farms.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?
The data pipeline and models are in Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch). The app is JavaScript (Node.js, React, Vite, Leaflet, Recharts, Tailwind) as a web app hosted on Vercel, built with Git, GitHub and assisted by Claude. 

Project Overview:

Field Shift v2 gives any US field its own crop rotation plan: what to plant, when, and why. It reads 40 years of NASA satellite and weather records for the exact field, learns how that field behaves, builds rotation options that fit it, tests each one through 40 real seasons and the 2040 climate, and recommends the plan that best matches the farmer's goals. Every answer states how sure it is and what to check with a local expert.

The system pairs two kinds of modeling. Trained machine-learning models (Models A to E) learn field-specific behavior from satellite and weather records. A transparent, daily process simulator, built on published agronomy (FAO-56, AquaCrop-style crop growth, RUSLE erosion), turns those learned parameters into water, nitrogen, soil, erosion, pest and profit outcomes a farmer can inspect. Unlike county-average tools, the unit of analysis is one field: soil, slope, weather and cropping history are all its own.

The system delivers two primary outputs:

  1. Rotation recommendation. Three side-by-side answers (most profitable, best balance, safest) chosen from 10 to 30 field-specific options plus the current rotation, each with six scores, four fit checks, a profit range, neighbor-field evidence, a confidence badge and a "Check locally" list.
  2. Farm simulator. The farmer starts from the field as it is today, changes crops, planting dates, fertilizer, irrigation, cover crops, prices or weather, and watches profit, soil, water and nutrients change day by day and month by month for one season up to 30 years.

Four design rules govern the build:

  • Every model output changes the recommendation, or it is cut.
  • One simulation engine powers both the recommendation and the simulator, so they always agree.
  • Every number comes with its uncertainty and its source.
  • The tool supports the farmer's judgment and local agricultural expertise; it never replaces them.

MATHEMATICAL FRAMEWORK

The simulator and optimizer use published agronomy equations so every answer can be explained; machine learning supplies the field-specific parameters. Notation: d is a day, s a simulated season, r a rotation, m a set of management choices, and r0, m0 the current rotation and practice.

Crop development and water use Growing degree days drive crop stages, and crop water use scales reference evapotranspiration by a stage-specific coefficient (FAO-56):

GDDd = max(0, (Tmax,d + Tmin,d) / 2 − Tbase)

ETc,d = Kc(stage) × ET0,d

The root-zone water balance is updated daily, starting from SMAP (or Model D) soil moisture:

Sd = Sd−1 + Pd + Id − ETc,d − Rd − Dd

(Where P is rain, I irrigation, R runoff, and D drainage).

Biomass and yield Growth is water-driven, in the style of FAO's AquaCrop model. Model B supplies this field's drought and heat sensitivity inside the stress factors, and Calibration E tunes the water productivity (WP*) and heat thresholds so simulated yields track NASS county yields:

B = WP* × Σd (Trd / ET0,d)

Y = HI × B × fheat × ffrost × fwater

Erosion, nitrogen and soil carbon Daily RUSLE estimates soil loss from this field's soil, slope, storm intensity and ground cover. A rotation is acceptable only if mean annual loss stays under the soil's tolerance T:

Ad = Rd × K × LS × Cd × P     Āyear ≤ T

(Where R is rain erosivity from IMERG storm intensity, K erodibility from gSSURGO, LS slope length and steepness from 3DEP, C ground cover from crop and residue, and P the practice factor).

Nitrogen is tracked as a daily balance, and soil organic matter with a two-pool carbon model:

Nd = Nd−1 + Md + Fd + Fixd − Ud − Ld

dC1/dt = aI − k1C1

dC2/dt = h k1C1 − k2C2

(Where M is mineralization, F fertilizer, Fix legume fixation, U crop uptake, L leaching, C1/C2 fast and slow carbon pools, I residue/root input, k decay rates, and h humified fraction).

Field state from satellites (Model A) Each day the field is in a hidden state z (green, residue or bare). A hidden Markov model recovers the state sequence from noisy observations o (NDVI, NDTI, BSI, radar):

P(z1:T | o1:T) ∝ π(z1) · b(o1 | z1) · ∏t=2T a(zt | zt−1) · b(ot | zt)

Profit and optimization Return above variable costs for season s is simulated yield times price for each harvest, minus variable costs, plus fertilizer saved by legume nitrogen credits:

πs(r, m) = Σh (Yh,s × ph,s) − Σj cj(r, m) + N credit savings

The optimizer searches rotations and management choices for the highest median profit inside the farmer's limits:

(r*, m*) = argmax(r,m) medians πs(r, m)

subject to Q0.10(π(r, m)) ≥ Q0.10(π(r0, m0)),   Ā(r, m) ≤ T,   no failed fit check

Uncertainty Model B's stress forecasts carry split-conformal ranges, which contain the true value at least 1 - alpha of the time:

Ĉ(x) = [ŷ(x) − q, ŷ(x) + q]     q = Quantile⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉/n(|yi − ŷi|)

Plan-level confidence comes from 1,000 Monte Carlo what-if runs. The share of runs in which the recommended plan beats the current rotation sets the badge:

Pbeat = (1 / 1000) × Σi=11000 1[π(i)(r*) > π(i)(r0)]

METHODOLOGY (NINE STEPS) Step 1: Pick the field USDA Crop Sequence Boundaries supply outline and crop history. Outside those outlines, the farmer draws the field. Optional farmer inputs override defaults.

Step 2: Build the field data cube 

Every dataset is converted to one row per field per day (simulator) and one row per field per month (models):

  • Fine grids (Landsat, HLS, Sentinel-1, ECOSTRESS): Mean of pixels inside the field, 45m in from edges; count of clear views kept.
  • Coarse grids (SMAP, IMERG, MODIS, Daymet): Area-weighted mean of overlapped cells; number of fields sharing a cell kept.
  • Very coarse (GRACE, CMIP6): Value at field location; used for trends and change, never for field differences.
  • Irregular passes: Monthly composites with observation counts; gaps marked missing, never zero-filled.
  • Sub-daily rain (IMERG): Daily total plus peak intensity.
  • Soil polygons (gSSURGO): Area-weighted mean over the field.

Step 3: Learn the field 

Four trained models and one calibration read the cube:

  • Model A (Field history): Gradient-boosted trees and 1D neural network for crop type; hidden Markov model for green, residue, or bare state.
  • Model B (Field response): Gradient-boosted trees with SHAP reasons and conformal 90% ranges for heat and drought response.
  • Model C (Climate regimes): Gaussian mixture, k-means, HMM over years to get scenario years and 2040 weights.
  • Model D (Moisture downscaling): Random forest or gradient boosting on terrain wetness, thermal, radar, soil against SMAP.
  • Calibration E (Calibration): Per-region tuning of crop water productivity and heat thresholds against NASS county yields.

Step 4: Build rotation options 

A crop library of 25 to 30 common US cash and cover crops evaluates temperature, frost, and water limits, bare windows from Model A, cover/second crop fitting, cash crop alternation, and rotation rules (change family every other year, include legume per cycle, no overlapping seasons).

Step 5: Run four fit checks

 Every option gets pass, warn, or fail on four checks:

  • Water: Fails if next crop starts short of water in > 1 of 4 years.
  • Disease: Fails if a cover hosts a serious pest of the next cash crop.
  • Market: Fails if almost no acres in county/neighbors and no buyer entered.
  • Season: Fails if it does not finish before next crop or frost in > 1 in 5 years.

Step 6: Simulate 

The field simulator runs every option day by day through all 40 past seasons and the 2040 climate (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 from NEX-GDDP-CMIP6).

Step 7: Optimize profit 

For each option, the optimizer tries planting date, nitrogen rate, variety maturity, cover termination date, double cropping, irrigation, and tillage using Bayesian optimization.

Step 8: Score, explain and recommend 

Six scores are weighted by farmer priorities. Three side-by-side answers are shown (most profitable, best balance, safest) with confidence badges, neighbor evidence, and "Check locally" lists.

Step 9: Validate 

Eight checks compare tool outputs against actual results: Model accuracy, bare days, crop dates, yields, erosion, soil moisture, neighbor backtest, and expert ranking.

  • Architecture: Modular design with Earth Engine data exports, data cube builder, crop library, Python simulator engine, models A-D, calibration E, optimizer, and backend API.
  • Performance Target: One simulated season runs in under 0.1 seconds; 40 seasons across several plans finish in a few seconds.
  • User Interface: Seven screens (Pick your field, Field story, Field risks, Options, Best plans, Farm simulator, Evidence and sources).

LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK

Current Limitations:

  • Expected outcomes, not forecasts (estimates from past weather and 2040 projections).
  • Regional costs (uses regional budgets/prices unless overridden).
  • Soil carbon is modeled, not measured.
  • Crop labels reliable mainly where mapped by USDA/WorldCereal.
  • Legume nitrogen credit varies and needs local verification.
  • Fit-check and badge thresholds are working defaults.
  • Model transfer limits outside tested regions.
  • Local factors (wet spots, drainage, water rights) require human input.

Future Improvements:

  1. Multi-region expansion across 8 to 10 US counties.
  2. Expert blind ranking validation.
  3. Model D soil moisture downscaling implementation.
  4. On-demand live analysis for any tapped field.
  5. Stronger crop engine evaluation (AquaCrop-OSPy).
  6. Farmer feedback loop for parameter improvement.
